Ottawa couple Jennifer and Mario Bazinet hold their baby girl Ava Belle and a photo of their son, Beau Paul, who died in December 2020. Analysts say Canada's slipping global ranking in infant deaths is a bright red warning flag about the state of the social safety net. (Little Wagon Photography)

Health policy experts and analysts say that's a red flag about the state of the country's social safety net, and that Canada's lower ranking reflects issues considered risk factors for infant deaths.These include lack of education and housing, poor access to food and health care, plus poverty and unemployment, according to the Pan-Canadian Health Inequalities Reporting Initiative.

In Canada, the [leading cause of infant deaths](https://data.oecd.org/healthstat/infant-mortality-rates.htm)are linked to low birth weight, birth defects, oxygen deprivation, infection and Sudden Infant Death Syndrome.

According to health policy experts, the rate of infant mortality is a key indicator of the overall health of a country's population.

*   [Quebec coroner links infant deaths in Nunavik to overcrowded housing](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/quebec-coroner-links-infant-deaths-nunavik-overcrowded-housing-1.6638272)
*   [Pregnant women in rural B.C. urged to leave town to deliver](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/rural-maternity-wards-1.4514289)

## 'Heartbreak on repeat'

![Image 6: An eight week old baby lies swaddled in grey in a cradle.](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.6777597,1678742019000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C3600%2C2384%29%3B)

Mario and Jennifer Bazinet's son, Beau Paul, at eight weeks old. His death at three and a half months was found to be a case of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome. (Stephanie de Montigny)

"This is heartbreaking. It's been heartbreak on repeat for patients and families and communities for many decades now. And I think we're seeing it only get worse," said Dr. Andrew Boozary, a primary care physician in Toronto and the executive director of Population Health and Social Medicine at the University Health Network.

Boozary says people often wrongly blame themselves for health outcomes that are driven by social determinants such as poverty or lack of access to health care.

"We have fundamentally worse health outcomes than almost all other [OECD] countries — other than the United States," he said.

"It's the willingness to accept these outcomes that I find is actually most damning … it cannot be any more stark than life and death for infants."

## How infant mortality rate is determined

Around the world, data is collected on infant mortality, which is defined as the death of children under one year old.This standard is used to report trends by [the Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality of Estimation,](https://data.oecd.org/healthstat/infant-mortality-rates.htm) which includes representatives from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations.

![Image 7: A man wearing a stethoscope looks at the camera. ](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.5609953,1680121271000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C621%2C3024%2C2594%29%3B)

Dr. Andrew Boozary says people often wrongly blame themselves for health outcomes driven by issues like poverty or lack of access to health care. (Ingrid Yu/UHN)

There are international variations in how that data is collected that critics say affects the rankings.

For instance, in Canada and the U.S., all babies that are born alive must be registered, but many European countries do not record babies who are born alive before they reach 24 weeks of gestational age in their overall infant mortality rate, according to [a 2012 study](https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/canada-s-rank-on-infant-mortality-index-called-unfair-1.1215259) by four Canadian universities and the Public Health Agency of Canada.

But even accounting for that, experts say Canada's slipping ranking is a warning sign.

## Ranking slipping for decades

Canada's trajectory is "striking," according to Dennis Raphael, a professor at the School of Health Policy and Management at York University.

In the past four decades Raphael notes that Canada has continually slipped in the rankings of infant mortality in [OECD](https://data.oecd.org/healthstat/infant-mortality-rates.htm) nations:from 10th out of 24 countries in 1980, to 26th out of 34 countries in 2011, and finally to 30th out of 38 countries in 2021.

* * *

Raphael, who is busy compiling the latest edition of the book he co-authoured,_The Social Determinants of Health: The Canadian Facts,_ calls that ranking "dismal."

The World Health Organization defines social determinants of health as the non-medical factors that influence health outcomes.

This includes everything from neighbourhoods and living conditions to the economic policies and funding for social supports.

*   [First Nations groups say police racism contributed to death of Sask. 13-month-old](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatoon/first-nations-groups-say-police-racism-contributed-death-baby-1.6370015)
*   [Baby in Sanirajak, Nunavut, dies after mom's call to health centre gets transferred to Iqaluit](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/sanirajak-baby-death-1.6766074)

## How systemic failures affect racialized families

Boozary noted that poverty and systemic racism are driving up preventable infant deaths. Research has shown that [systemic failures](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6832817/) hit low income and racialized families the hardest.

"It's a national concern," he said.

By 2021 the Canadian [non-Indigenous infant mortality rate](https://data.oecd.org/healthstat/infant-mortality-rates.htm)was 4.4 deaths per 1,000 births. The Indigenous infant mortality rate was more than twice that, at 9.2 deaths per 1,000 births.

"We've got an infant mortality issue," said Raphael, noting that high infant mortality rates in Canada are usually framed as an Indigenous issue, as rates for Indigenous infants are more than double non-Indigenous mortality rates.

"I was able to find the infant mortality rate from a Canadian government document for non-Indigenous, and we're still pretty bad."

*   [Racism a barrier to prenatal health care, midwives say](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/midwife-racism-prenatal-health-care-conference-1.4867236)
*   [Social factors having greater negative impact on health of First Nations people, northern Manitobans](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/social-determinants-health-first-nations-northern-manitoba-1.6693246)

Dr. Janet Smylie, a Métis physician and research scientist who is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Advancing Generative Health Services for Indigenous Populations in Canada, says infant death is a measure of the health of a society.

"It's a loss of potential. And we know that it's linked to equity measures," she said.

There have been numerous studies linking high infant mortality to [systemic racism](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6832817/) and [other inequalities](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/science-research-data/inequalities-infant-mortality-infographic.html) such as poverty and [lack of access to health care](https://www.ohrc.on.ca/en/race-policy-dialogue-papers/racial-inequality-access-health-care-services).

![Image 8: A woman with grey hair in a ponytail uses a stethoscope. ](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.2942669,1680146557000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1920%2C1080%29%3B)

Dr. Janet Smylie, a Métis physician and research scientist, says infant death is a measure of the health of a society. (CBC)

Smylie said the number of Indigenous infants that die is likely an undercount due to the lack of quality data collected, leading to a failure to recognize some infants as Indigenous.

"It could quite well be that disparities in First Nations, Inuit and Métis infant mortality are still driving this," she said. "But we don't know because we don't have quality information about infant mortality or birth weight in this country."

## Low birth weights

The rate of infants born at low birth weights — another good predictor of underlying health issues — has also worsened in the past decade, according to health policy analysts.

Canada's comparative performance for low birth weight rate slipped from 12th out of 34 OECD nations in 2013 to 19th out of 37 nations by 2019.

Infant birth weights that are lower or higher than the average can be predictive of health issues that can persist into adulthood.

*   [How Indigenous people are rebuilding child welfare to lift up the whole family](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/unreserved/how-indigenous-people-are-rebuilding-child-welfare-to-lift-up-the-whole-family-1.6364460)

A baby's birth weight is affected by many factors, including the mother's stress levels and nutrition and health concerns, such as diabetes. In Canada, the average newborn weighs about 3.5 kilograms (7.5 pounds),although between 2.5 kilograms(5.5 pounds)and 4.5 kilograms(10 pounds) is considered[within the normal range](https://myhealth.alberta.ca/Health/Pages/conditions.aspx?hwid=te6295#:~:text=The%20average%20birth%20weight%20for,a%20little%20heavier%20than%20girls.).

According to a Stats Canada study of close to six million births in Canada released in January 2022, the average birth weight of babies [decreased](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/82-003-x/2022001/article/00001-eng.htm)between 2002 and 2016.

When it comes to Canada's low infant mortality ranking, Raphael believes it is a "canary in the coal mine" signifying other problems with Canadian institutions overall —from the strained health-care system and a lack of social supports, to low wages that haven't kept up with the cost of living.

Raphael and Boozary suggest the best way to counter these rates and reverse the country's slipping ranking is to stop chipping away at those social programs and instead concentrate on pre-natal care by providing better access to health care and family doctors, and working to improve housing, food insecurity, wages and mental health supports.

Around the world, data is collected on infant mortality, which is defined as the death of children under one year old.This standard is used to report trends by [the Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality of Estimation,](https://data.oecd.org/healthstat/infant-mortality-rates.htm) which includes representatives from the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations.

![Image 7: A man wearing a stethoscope looks at the camera. ](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.5609953,1680121271000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C621%2C3024%2C2594%29%3B)

Dr. Andrew Boozary says people often wrongly blame themselves for health outcomes driven by issues like poverty or lack of access to health care. (Ingrid Yu/UHN)

There are international variations in how that data is collected that critics say affects the rankings.

For instance, in Canada and the U.S., all babies that are born alive must be registered, but many European countries do not record babies who are born alive before they reach 24 weeks of gestational age in their overall infant mortality rate, according to [a 2012 study](https://www.cbc.ca/news/health/canada-s-rank-on-infant-mortality-index-called-unfair-1.1215259) by four Canadian universities and the Public Health Agency of Canada.

But even accounting for that, experts say Canada's slipping ranking is a warning sign.

## Ranking slipping for decades

Canada's trajectory is "striking," according to Dennis Raphael, a professor at the School of Health Policy and Management at York University.

In the past four decades Raphael notes that Canada has continually slipped in the rankings of infant mortality in [OECD](https://data.oecd.org/healthstat/infant-mortality-rates.htm) nations:from 10th out of 24 countries in 1980, to 26th out of 34 countries in 2011, and finally to 30th out of 38 countries in 2021.

* * *

Raphael, who is busy compiling the latest edition of the book he co-authoured,_The Social Determinants of Health: The Canadian Facts,_ calls that ranking "dismal."

The World Health Organization defines social determinants of health as the non-medical factors that influence health outcomes.

This includes everything from neighbourhoods and living conditions to the economic policies and funding for social supports.

*   [First Nations groups say police racism contributed to death of Sask. 13-month-old](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatoon/first-nations-groups-say-police-racism-contributed-death-baby-1.6370015)
*   [Baby in Sanirajak, Nunavut, dies after mom's call to health centre gets transferred to Iqaluit](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/sanirajak-baby-death-1.6766074)

## How systemic failures affect racialized families

Boozary noted that poverty and systemic racism are driving up preventable infant deaths. Research has shown that [systemic failures](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6832817/) hit low income and racialized families the hardest.

"It's a national concern," he said.

By 2021 the Canadian [non-Indigenous infant mortality rate](https://data.oecd.org/healthstat/infant-mortality-rates.htm)was 4.4 deaths per 1,000 births. The Indigenous infant mortality rate was more than twice that, at 9.2 deaths per 1,000 births.

"We've got an infant mortality issue," said Raphael, noting that high infant mortality rates in Canada are usually framed as an Indigenous issue, as rates for Indigenous infants are more than double non-Indigenous mortality rates.

"I was able to find the infant mortality rate from a Canadian government document for non-Indigenous, and we're still pretty bad."

*   [Racism a barrier to prenatal health care, midwives say](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/midwife-racism-prenatal-health-care-conference-1.4867236)
*   [Social factors having greater negative impact on health of First Nations people, northern Manitobans](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/manitoba/social-determinants-health-first-nations-northern-manitoba-1.6693246)

Dr. Janet Smylie, a Métis physician and research scientist who is a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Advancing Generative Health Services for Indigenous Populations in Canada, says infant death is a measure of the health of a society.

"It's a loss of potential. And we know that it's linked to equity measures," she said.

There have been numerous studies linking high infant mortality to [systemic racism](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6832817/) and [other inequalities](https://www.canada.ca/en/public-health/services/publications/science-research-data/inequalities-infant-mortality-infographic.html) such as poverty and [lack of access to health care](https://www.ohrc.on.ca/en/race-policy-dialogue-papers/racial-inequality-access-health-care-services).

![Image 8: A woman with grey hair in a ponytail uses a stethoscope. ](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.2942669,1680146557000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1920%2C1080%29%3B)

Dr. Janet Smylie, a Métis physician and research scientist, says infant death is a measure of the health of a society. (CBC)

Smylie said the number of Indigenous infants that die is likely an undercount due to the lack of quality data collected, leading to a failure to recognize some infants as Indigenous.

"It could quite well be that disparities in First Nations, Inuit and Métis infant mortality are still driving this," she said. "But we don't know because we don't have quality information about infant mortality or birth weight in this country."

## Low birth weights

The rate of infants born at low birth weights — another good predictor of underlying health issues — has also worsened in the past decade, according to health policy analysts.

Canada's comparative performance for low birth weight rate slipped from 12th out of 34 OECD nations in 2013 to 19th out of 37 nations by 2019.

Infant birth weights that are lower or higher than the average can be predictive of health issues that can persist into adulthood.

*   [How Indigenous people are rebuilding child welfare to lift up the whole family](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/unreserved/how-indigenous-people-are-rebuilding-child-welfare-to-lift-up-the-whole-family-1.6364460)

A baby's birth weight is affected by many factors, including the mother's stress levels and nutrition and health concerns, such as diabetes. In Canada, the average newborn weighs about 3.5 kilograms (7.5 pounds),although between 2.5 kilograms(5.5 pounds)and 4.5 kilograms(10 pounds) is considered[within the normal range](https://myhealth.alberta.ca/Health/Pages/conditions.aspx?hwid=te6295#:~:text=The%20average%20birth%20weight%20for,a%20little%20heavier%20than%20girls.).

According to a Stats Canada study of close to six million births in Canada released in January 2022, the average birth weight of babies [decreased](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/82-003-x/2022001/article/00001-eng.htm)between 2002 and 2016.

When it comes to Canada's low infant mortality ranking, Raphael believes it is a "canary in the coal mine" signifying other problems with Canadian institutions overall —from the strained health-care system and a lack of social supports, to low wages that haven't kept up with the cost of living.

Raphael and Boozary suggest the best way to counter these rates and reverse the country's slipping ranking is to stop chipping away at those social programs and instead concentrate on pre-natal care by providing better access to health care and family doctors, and working to improve housing, food insecurity, wages and mental health supports.

## Abstract

### Background

Low birth weight continues to be a significant cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, contributing to 80% of neonatal deaths in low and middle-income countries. To the authors’ knowledge, no prior study has estimated the regional and sub-regional prevalence of low birth weight and its determinants in these settings. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the pooled and regional estimates of low birth weight in low and middle-income countries.

### Methods

We used a weighted sample of 343,898 birth records, taken from the pooled demographic and health surveys conducted from 2015 to 2022 in 44 low and middle-income countries. Overall and sub-regional trends in low birth weight estimates were presented using a line graph. A multilevel mixed-effect analysis was done to identify determinants of low birth weight. Model comparison was performed using deviance and log-likelihood values, and statistical significance was determined at a P-value of less than 0.05.

### Results

The overall prevalence of low birth weight births was 13.7% [95% CI: 13.5%—13.8%], showing significant variations among countries and regions. Asia region had the highest prevalence at 16%, followed by Latin America, the Caribbean, and Europe at 11.5%, and Africa at 9.5%. Our study also indicated a decline in low birth weight from 11.4% to 9.5% over eight-year periods, with no consistent trend observed. Furthermore, factors such as health insurance, household wealth, maternal age, access to healthcare facilities, maternal education, neonate’s sex, prenatal care, and antenatal iron supplementation were found to be statistically associated with low birth weight.

### Conclusion

Our findings highlight the significant burden of low birth weight births, with notable variations in rates among countries and regions. The study also reveals a slight decline in low birth weight over time, although no consistent trend was observed. Importantly, maternal and household factors play significant roles in influencing low birth weight. Thus, addressing these factors through targeted interventions and policies could help reduce the incidence of low birth weight births in LMICs.

## Background

Low birth weight (LBW) continues to be a significant cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality. World Health Organization (WHO) reported that about 80% of neonatal deaths in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) are attributed to LBW [1]. Furthermore, it is linked to various short-term and long-term complications during childhood and adulthood periods, and this impact is pronounced in resource-constrained settings, where access to quality healthcare is limited [2, 3].

According to WHO and the United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund estimates, 15% to 20% of live births worldwide have LBW, and 91% of these births occur in LMICs [4]. In sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), the incidence of LBW is significantly higher compared to other regions [5], where 13% of babies are born with low birth weight [6].

Studies in different settings have shown a strong link between LBW and socioeconomic status in LMICs. Factors such as poverty, educational attainment, healthcare accessibility, and living conditions profoundly influence the occurrence of LBW [5, 7]. Additionally, there is a heightened risk of LBW among disadvantaged populations [8, 9], those with limited access to prenatal care, inadequate nutrition, exposure to environmental toxins, and elevated stress levels [10]. Furthermore, disparities in healthcare services were reported to exacerbate the impact of socioeconomic status on LBW (Fig.1) [11].Fig. 1Conceptual framework of factors associated with low birth weight

In the pursuit of achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030, several interventions have been proposed to address LBW and reduce child mortality [12]. These interventions include targeted antenatal care, nutritional counseling during pregnancy, and the encouragement of institutional deliveries [12, 13]. However, to develop effective strategies, robust evidence on trends in the prevalence of LBW across different contexts and the relationship between LBW and socioeconomic factors is crucial.

Despite its public health significance, current evidence of LBW on comprehensive data aggregation across LMICs is limited. Unfortunately, previous studies on LBW across developing regions were limited to specific geographic areas and failed to indicate the trends in this adverse neonatal outcome [5, 14–16]. To our knowledge, no prior study has estimated the regional and sub-regional prevalence of LBW and its socio-economic determinants in LMICs. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the pooled and regional estimates of LBW across 44 LMICs using demographic and health survey (DHS) data.

## Methods

### Study design and data source

We conducted a secondary analysis of cross-sectional data obtained from the most recent demographic and health surveys carried out from 2015 to 2022 in 44 low- and middle-income countries. The analysis included 25 countries from Africa, 15 from Asia, and 4 from other regions such as Latin America, Caribbean, and Europe.

### Study population and sample size

Initially, a total of 1,472,525 birth records (neonates) were identified in the 44 surveys appended for analysis, of which 991,581 had a missing observation on birth weight, 110,050 neonates were not weighed at birth, and 25,596 had unknown birth weight. After dropping records with missing observations and those with no birth weight data, a weighted sample of 343,898 birth records (unweighted sample size = 345,298) was included in the final analysis. ### Variables

#### Dependent variable

In this study, the dependent variable was birth weight, which was generated from the birth weight data measured in grams”. Thus, birth weights of less than 2500 g, 2500–3999 g, and > 4000 g were classified as low birth weight, normal birth weight, and excessive birth weight (macrosomia), respectively. We used the two classifications (low birth weight and others) for multivariable mixed-effect logistic regression model to identify the correlates of low birth weight. And we used three classifications for descriptive statistics to show the proportion of each class of birth weight in each country and region.

#### Independent variables

Individual-level variables included mother’s age, marital status, education and, media exposure, wealth index, coverage by health insurance, sex of neonate, age at marriage, parity, birth order, preceding birth interval, number of antenatal care (ANC) visits, timing of ANC visits, use of iron folic acid supplements, and history of pregnancy termination. While, region, residence, and distance to health facility were considered as the community-level variables.

Media exposure was computed using three variables (frequency of watching television, listening to the radio, and reading newspapers) that have three response options (i.e. not at all, less than once a week, and at least once a week). Thus, women who reported watching television, listening to the radio, or reading the newspaper at least once a week were considered as having media exposure and otherwise labeled as not having exposure to mass media.

### Data management and statistical analysis

Data cleaning and analysis were conducted using Stata software version 17. Prior to analysis, the presence of the outcome variable (i.e. weight at birth) in the DHS dataset for each country was confirmed, and all study variables were assessed for missing data. Birth records with missing observation and unknown birth weight, and those not weighted at birth were dropped from the analysis. Finally, the datasets of 44 LMIC countries were appended and weighted to compensate for the non-representativeness of the sample and obtain reliable estimates and standard errors.

To account for the hierarchical nature of DHS design, a multilevel logistic regression analysis was applied to determine the effects of independent variables on low birth weight. Initially, bivariable multilevel logistic regression analysis was done and variables with a p-value of less than 0.25 in this analysis were selected for the multivariable regression model.

### Fixed-effect multilevel analysis

Four hierarchical models were independently fitted to select the model that best fits the data. To test the random variability in the intercept, an empty model i.e. a model without an independent variable was fitted. In the second and third models, the effect of individual and community level variables on low birth weight was respectively assessed, while the combined effect of both community and individual level variables on the outcome variable was simultaneously assessed in the fourth model.

_Model I (empty model)_: in this model, the likelihood of low birth weight is only a function of the clusters in which the neonates reside, which is indicated by a random intercept at the cluster level:

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}\;(\mathrm{pi})=\log\;\mathrm{odds}=\left[\frac{\mathrm{pi}}{1\;-\;\mathrm{pi}}\right]\;=\;\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = log odds = \left[\frac{pi}{1 - pi}\right] = M + E_{A}
$$

Where M = overall mean prevalence of low birth weight expressed on the logistic scale. EA = cluster level residuals normally distributed on the logistic scale with a mean of 0 and a variance of VA. VA = the cluster residual variance represents the variability around the overall prevalence (M) on the logistic scale.

_Model II (a model with individual-level variables)_: this model measured the probability of low birth weight as a function of the cluster in which the neonates live and maternal and child characteristics (e.g. sex of child, maternal age, maternal education…etc.).

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}(\mathrm{pi})\;=\;\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_1\mathrm{sex}\;\mathrm{of}\;{\mathrm{child}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_2\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{age}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_3\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{education}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;\mathrm\beta4\dots\;.\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = M + \beta_{1} sex of child_{i} + \beta_{2} maternal age_{i} + \beta_{3} maternal education_{i} + \beta 4 \hdots . + E_{A}
$$

Where β is the regression coefficient of each individual-level variable included in this model.

_Model III (model with community-level variables)_: this model assessed the probability of low birth weight as a function of cluster and community-level variables (e.g. Region, residence, and distance to health facility).

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}(\mathrm{pi})=\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_1{\mathrm{region}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_2{\mathrm{residence}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_3{\mathrm{distance}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = M + \beta_{1} region_{i} + \beta_{2} residence_{i} + \beta_{3} distance_{i} + E_{A}
$$

Where β is the regression coefficient of each community-level variable included in this model.

_Model IV (model with both individual and community-level variables)_: in this model, the combined effect of both individual and community-level variables on the occurrence of low birth weight was simultaneously assessed.

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}(\mathrm{pi})\;=\;\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_1\mathrm{sex}\;\mathrm{of}\;{\mathrm{child}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_2\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{age}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_3\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{education}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;\mathrm\beta4\dots\;.{\mathrm\beta}_5{\mathrm{region}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_6{\mathrm{residence}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_7{\mathrm{distance}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = M + \beta_{1} sex of child_{i} + \beta_{2} maternal age_{i} + \beta_{3} maternal education_{i} + \beta 4 \hdots . \beta_{5} region_{i} + \beta_{6} residence_{i} + \beta_{7} distance_{i} + E_{A}
$$

After fitting these models, models were compared based on log-likelihood (LL) and deviance (i.e. −2*LL) values to select the one that best fits the data. For instance, model IV has the lowest deviance and highest LL values and is hence considered as the best-fitted model for the final analysis. A generalized variance inflation factor [GVIF = VIF[1/(2*df)] was used to determine the presence of collinearity between explanatory variables and this value was less than five for all variables included in the final model, suggesting the non-existence of multi-collinearity. Finally, in the multivariable analysis, a _p_-value less than 0.05 and an adjusted odds ratio with the corresponding 95% confidence interval were used to identify determinants of low birth weight.

### Random-effect analysis (measures of variance)

Random variability in the level of low birth weight across clusters was estimated by intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC), proportion change in variance (PCV), and median odds ratio (MOR). In this analysis, ICC indicates the total variance in the proportion of low birth weight attributed to cluster differences. ICC was estimated by:

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{ICC}\;=\;\frac{{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}}{{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}\;+\;{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm i}}$\end{document}

$$
ICC = \frac{V_{a}}{V_{a} + V_{i}}
$$

Where, V a = cluster level variance and Vi = individual level variance.

PCV (attributable percentage variability in the multilevel model) measured the differences in the prevalence of low birth weight attributed to community or individual-level characteristics.

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{PCV}=\frac{\left[{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}\;-\;{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm b}\right]}{{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}}$\end{document}

$$
PCV = \frac{\left[V_{a}, ,-, ,V_{b}\right]}{V_{a}}
$$

Where V a = the variance of the empty model and V b = the variance of other models.

Heterogeneity in the risk of low birth weight among neonates in different clusters was assessed by MOR. It was measured as the median value of the odds of the outcome variable (i.e. low birth weight) between neonates living in the area at the highest risk of low birth weight compared to those in the clusters at the lowest risk of the event. MOR was computed using the following formula:

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{MOR}\;=\;\exp\;\left\{\sqrt{2\mathrm\tau}_0^2\mathrm\Phi\left(0.75\right)\right\}$\end{document}

$$
MOR = exp \left{\sqrt{2 \tau}_{0}^{2},\Phi,\left(0.75\right)\right}
$$

Where, Φ is the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal distribution, and Φ*(0.75) ~ 0.6745.

### Ethical approval

Data were obtained from a demographic and health survey, and permission to access it was granted through an online request process available at [http://www.dhsprogram.com](http://www.dhsprogram.com/). The accessed data were solely utilized for this registered study and can be publicly accessed from the program’s official database.

### Pooled and regional estimates of low birth weight in LMICs

Our analysis revealed that the overall prevalence of low birth weight births in low- and middle-income countries was estimated to be 13.7% [95% CI: 13.5%—13.8%], with significant variations across countries and regions. This finding indicates that, during the period from 2015 to 2022, there were a total of 46,988 low birth weight births recorded across 44 LMICs. The countries with the highest prevalence were Mauritania (25.0%), Pakistan (22.8%), India (17.7%), Haiti (17.1%), and Jordan (16.6%), while the lowest prevalence was observed in Sierra Leone (4.8%), Albania (4.9%), Armenia (5.7%), and Cambodia (6.1%). Regionally, Asia had the highest proportion of low birth weight births at 16%, followed by Latin America, the Caribbean, and Europe at 11.5%, and Africa at 9.5% (Fig.2).Fig. 2Regional and sub-regional estimates of low birth weight across 44 LMICs, 2015–2022

### Trend in low and excessive birth weight across 44 LMICs from 2015 to 2022

To examine the trend in the level of abnormal birth weight across 44 LMICs since 2015, countries were grouped based on the year of the survey. In this regard, from the surveys included in the analysis, six were conducted in 2015, eight in 2016, five in 2017, twelve in 2018/19, three in 2020, five in 2021, and six in 2022. Figure3 illustrates that the prevalence of low, excessive, and overall abnormal birth weight declined from 11.4% to 9.5%, 6.9% to 3.9%, and 18.3% to 13.5%, respectively over eight eight-year periods. However, the observed change did not follow consistent patterns, indicated by an increase in macrosomia by more than two-fold between 2021 and 2022 and an increase in the levels of both low and abnormal birth weight between 2020 and 2021 (Fig.3).Fig. 3Trend in low birth weight, macrosomia, and abnormal birth weight across 44 LMICs from 2015 to 2022

### Trend in low and excessive birth weight in 25 SSA countries from 2015 to 2022

Figure4 illustrates changes in birth weight across survey years in 25 African countries included in the analysis. For instance, both low and excessive birth weight declined from 10.2% to 8.5% and 8.3% to 5.2% over the survey periods respectively, however, the observed change was minimal for low birth weight compared to macrosomia. The result indicates that the most significant drop in low birth weight occurred between 2021 and 2022, while the largest decline of 50% in excessive birth weight was observed between 2016 and 2017 (Fig.4).Fig. 4Trend in low birth weight, macrosomia, and abnormal birth weight across 25 SSA countries from 2015 to 2022

### Trend in low and excessive birth weight in 15 Asian countries from 2015 to 2022

Variations in low and excessive birth weight in 15 Asian countries over different survey years are presented in Fig.5 below. The result revealed that consistent with changes observed in the African region, the trend in both abnormal birth weight indices has followed up-and-down patterns, with low birth weight decreasing from 15.8% to 10.9%, and excessive birth weight declining from 10.6% to 2.35%. Additionally, the results also underscore a consistent rise in the proportion of low birth weight births over three survey periods spanning from 2017 to 2021 (Fig.5).Fig. 5Trend in low birth weight, macrosomia, and abnormal birth weight across 15 Asian countries from 2015 to 2022

### Low and excessive birth weight across maternal characteristics

Figure6 shows the distribution of both low and excessive birth weight across maternal education and household wealth index. The analysis indicated a decrease in the proportion of low birth weight births as maternal age increases, dropping from 15.7% among younger women to 11.8% among those older than 34 years. On the contrary, the prevalence of excessive birth weight has increased as maternal age advances. Additionally, our findings highlighted a decline in low birth weight and a slight increase in macrosomic births with an improved household wealth index (Fig.6).Fig. 6Distribution of low and excessive birth weight across maternal age (**a**) and household wealth (**b**) in LMICs, 2015–2022

The result in Fig.7 shows a rise in the proportion of neonates with low birth weight as parity increases, with rates at 15.5% for first-time mothers compared to 11.8% for grand-multiparous women. Conversely, there was an uptick trend in the occurrences of macrosomic and overall abnormal birth weight births as parity progressed, with rates of 8.3% and 20.1% among grand-multiparous women, respectively. Additionally, our results indicate a decrease in both low and excessive birth weight births and their combinations as the frequency of antenatal visits increases (Fig.7).Fig. 7Distribution of low and excessive birth weight across maternal parity (**a**) and number of ANC visits (**b**) in LMICs, 2015–2022

### Measures of variation (Random-effect analysis)

The result of random effects analysis showed that 16% of the variability in low birth weight prevalence was due to differences at the cluster level (ICC values of model I), while 20% of the variability was explained by both individual and community-level factors (ICC values of model IV). The percentage change in variance (PCV) value of model IV indicated that the combined influence of individual and community-level variables explained 20% of the variation in low birth weight estimates. Additionally, the measure of association (MOR) of 2.44 in the empty model suggested heterogeneity in the proportion of low birth weight births across clusters. This means that infants in clusters with higher rates of low birth weight were 2.44 times more likely to have a birth weight below the normal range compared to those in clusters with lower rates ### Determinants of low birth weight in LMICs (Fixed-effect analysis)

After adjusting for the potential covariates, the result of a multilevel mixed-effect regression analysis showed a significant correlation between maternal characteristics and low birth weight. For instance, being not covered by health insurance [AOR (95% CI): 1.12 [1.06–1.18]], poor household wealth [AOR (95% CI): 1.15 [1.09–1.22]], younger maternal age [AOR (95% CI): 1.11 [1.02–1.21]], and facing challenges in accessing health facility [AOR (95% CI): 1.15 [1.11–1.19] were positively linked to low birth weight. Likewise, neonates born to mothers with no formal education [AOR (95% CI): 1.47 [1.33–1.63]], primary education [AOR (95% CI): 1.31 [1.19–1.44]], and secondary education [AOR (95% CI): 1.22 [1.12–1.33]] were at an increased risk of having low birth weight compared to those born to mothers with higher educational attainment. Furthermore, the analysis revealed that compared to their counter groups, neonates of mothers who did not receive prenatal care [AOR (95% CI): 1.35 [1.20–1.53]] or did not take antenatal iron supplementation [AOR (95% CI): 1.26 [1.10–1.45]] were about 35% and 26% more likely to have birth weight below the normal range, respectively (Table4).

## Discussion

The result showed that the pooled estimate of low birth weight in LMICs was 13.7% [95% CI: 13.5%—13.8%], with the highest prevalence in Mauritania (25.0%) and lowest in Sierra Leone (4.8%). This finding is consistent with the result of a study in six LMICs (13.6%) [14]. However, our finding is higher than the result of a study in 35 SSA countries (9.8%) [5], but slightly lower than the 2015 global estimate of 14.6% [4, 17]. The discrepancy between the results could be due to differences in data collection methods, sample sizes, or population demographics. Additionally, the slight variation from the global estimate could be due to regional differences in healthcare systems and socio-economic factors impacting maternal and child health outcomes.

The results of this study also show that beyond the individual characteristics of the participants, low birth weight is explained by contextual factors. For instance, the analysis revealed that newborns from households without health insurance had a 12% higher likelihood of being born with low birth weight compared to those born in households with health insurance coverage. This finding is supported by the previous studies that reported a significant link between health insurance coverage and reduced risk of low birth weight [18–20]. The most possible justification for this association is that women not enrolled in health insurance programs may not receive adequate prenatal care due to their lower socioeconomic status, which can directly affect pregnancy outcomes.

The sex of the neonates was also identified as one of the significant variables predicting low birth weight. For instance, compared to males, female neonates had a 30% higher likelihood of having low birth weight. Consistent with this finding, studies in SSA [5, 15] and a systematic review in Ethiopia [21] reported a higher risk of low birth weight among female neonates. This could be explained by the biological differences in fetal growth and development between genders. Studies have shown that female fetuses tend to have slower growth rates than males, which may increase their exposure to LBW [22].

Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the likelihood of low birth weight was 15% higher for newborns in poor households compared to those in rich households. Consistent with this, previous studies in different settings indicated a higher risk of low birth weight among neonates belonging to families of lower socioeconomic status [7, 15, 23, 24]. Socioeconomic disparities that can impact access to quality healthcare, nutrition, and overall living conditions can explain this finding. For instance, women in poor households may have limited access to prenatal care, inadequate nutrition, and higher levels of stress, which may result in poor pregnancy outcomes. Moreover, women from lower-income households are more likely to experience food insecurity and have limited access to essential nutrients during pregnancy, which can affect fetal growth and development.

Similar to the results of the studies conducted in SSA [15] and Kenya [25], this study found that infants of mothers who had difficulty accessing the nearest health facility were more likely to have babies with low birth weight when compared to their counterparts. This might be because women who face challenges in accessing healthcare facilities may experience delays in receiving essential prenatal care, screenings, and interventions, which can contribute to adverse birth outcomes such as LBW [26].

Lower maternal education was linked with an increased risk of low birth weight. The result showed that the risk of low birth weight was increased by 47%, 31%, and 22% for neonates born to mothers with no education, primary education, and secondary education, respectively. This finding is consistent with the previous studies in which maternal literacy was reported as a protective factor for low birth weight [5, 15, 27, 28]. This association could be because mothers with higher education may have better access to healthcare services and information that can promote healthier pregnancies and better birth outcomes. Additionally, higher education may be associated with greater knowledge about nutrition, prenatal care, and overall health practices that can positively impact fetal growth and development [29].

In addition, our analysis revealed that compared to their reference groups, neonates of mothers who did not have prenatal care were 1.35 times more likely to be born with low birth weight. Similarly, a study conducted in Ethiopia demonstrated that non-attendance of ANC was associated with an increased risk of LBW [21]. Likewise, other previous studies in African settings [5, 14, 15] found the attendance of antenatal care as a protective factor against LBW. This can be explained by the fact that the absence of prenatal care can lead to missed opportunities for interventions and support that are essential for promoting healthy pregnancies and reducing the risk of adverse outcomes such as LBW.

Prenatal nutritional supplementation was also identified as another important factor linked with low birth weight. The study showed that babies born to mothers who did not receive iron supplementation during pregnancy had a higher risk of low birth weight compared to those whose mothers took the supplement. This finding is consistent with studies conducted in Ethiopia, which indicated a lower chance of low birth weight among infants born to mothers who received this nutritional supplementation during pregnancy [11, 30]. This might be because maternal iron deficiency during pregnancy can lead to inadequate oxygen supply to the fetus, which may result in restricted growth [31].

### Strength and limitations

This study has several notable strengths, such as the utilization of a larger sample size, nationally representative multi-country data from 44 countries, and application of advanced statistical methods i.e. multilevel modeling to account for the nested structure of the DHS data. However, it is important to consider certain limitations when interpreting the findings. These include potential over or underestimation of estimates due to a large number of missing birth weight data in the original dataset, and differences in the number of countries and sample sizes in the regions included in the analysis might affect the regional estimates. Additionally, the study did not assess the influence of preconception and antenatal maternal nutritional status on the outcome variable due to a lack of available data in the DHS.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, the overall prevalence of LBW in LMICs was 13.7%, with notable variations in rates among countries and regions and a slight decline over time. The findings also showed that lack of health insurance, poor household wealth, younger maternal age, limited access to healthcare facilities, lower educational attainment, and inadequate prenatal care and iron supplementation were associated with an increased risk of LBW.

The reduction in LBW rates over eight years signifies some positive change, but the inconsistent patterns along with pre-existing socioeconomic and healthcare accessibility challenges highlight the need for context-specific actions. Important modifiable factors such as maternal education, prenatal care, antenatal iron supplements, and household wealth point toward the necessity of lowering structural imbalance and better maternal health services. Additionally, our finding suggests the need to focus on high-burden areas to lower LBW and the associated future health impacts.

## Abstract

### Background

Low birth weight continues to be a significant cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, contributing to 80% of neonatal deaths in low and middle-income countries. To the authors’ knowledge, no prior study has estimated the regional and sub-regional prevalence of low birth weight and its determinants in these settings. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the pooled and regional estimates of low birth weight in low and middle-income countries.

### Methods

We used a weighted sample of 343,898 birth records, taken from the pooled demographic and health surveys conducted from 2015 to 2022 in 44 low and middle-income countries. Overall and sub-regional trends in low birth weight estimates were presented using a line graph. A multilevel mixed-effect analysis was done to identify determinants of low birth weight. Model comparison was performed using deviance and log-likelihood values, and statistical significance was determined at a P-value of less than 0.05.

### Results

The overall prevalence of low birth weight births was 13.7% [95% CI: 13.5%—13.8%], showing significant variations among countries and regions. Asia region had the highest prevalence at 16%, followed by Latin America, the Caribbean, and Europe at 11.5%, and Africa at 9.5%. Our study also indicated a decline in low birth weight from 11.4% to 9.5% over eight-year periods, with no consistent trend observed. Furthermore, factors such as health insurance, household wealth, maternal age, access to healthcare facilities, maternal education, neonate’s sex, prenatal care, and antenatal iron supplementation were found to be statistically associated with low birth weight.

### Conclusion

Our findings highlight the significant burden of low birth weight births, with notable variations in rates among countries and regions. The study also reveals a slight decline in low birth weight over time, although no consistent trend was observed. Importantly, maternal and household factors play significant roles in influencing low birth weight. Thus, addressing these factors through targeted interventions and policies could help reduce the incidence of low birth weight births in LMICs.

**Keywords:**Low and middle-income countries, Low birth weight, Demographic and Health Survey, Determinants, Multilevel analysis

## Background

Low birth weight (LBW) continues to be a significant cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality. World Health Organization (WHO) reported that about 80% of neonatal deaths in low and middle-income countries (LMICs) are attributed to LBW [1]. Furthermore, it is linked to various short-term and long-term complications during childhood and adulthood periods, and this impact is pronounced in resource-constrained settings, where access to quality healthcare is limited [2, 3].

According to WHO and the United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund estimates, 15% to 20% of live births worldwide have LBW, and 91% of these births occur in LMICs [4]. In sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), the incidence of LBW is significantly higher compared to other regions [5], where 13% of babies are born with low birth weight [6].

Studies in different settings have shown a strong link between LBW and socioeconomic status in LMICs. Factors such as poverty, educational attainment, healthcare accessibility, and living conditions profoundly influence the occurrence of LBW [5, 7]. Additionally, there is a heightened risk of LBW among disadvantaged populations [8, 9], those with limited access to prenatal care, inadequate nutrition, exposure to environmental toxins, and elevated stress levels [10]. Furthermore, disparities in healthcare services were reported to exacerbate the impact of socioeconomic status on LBW (Fig.1) [11].Fig. 1Conceptual framework of factors associated with low birth weight

In the pursuit of achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030, several interventions have been proposed to address LBW and reduce child mortality [12]. These interventions include targeted antenatal care, nutritional counseling during pregnancy, and the encouragement of institutional deliveries [12, 13]. However, to develop effective strategies, robust evidence on trends in the prevalence of LBW across different contexts and the relationship between LBW and socioeconomic factors is crucial.

Despite its public health significance, current evidence of LBW on comprehensive data aggregation across LMICs is limited. Unfortunately, previous studies on LBW across developing regions were limited to specific geographic areas and failed to indicate the trends in this adverse neonatal outcome [5, 14–16]. To our knowledge, no prior study has estimated the regional and sub-regional prevalence of LBW and its socio-economic determinants in LMICs. Therefore, this study aimed to examine the pooled and regional estimates of LBW across 44 LMICs using demographic and health survey (DHS) data.

## Methods

### Study design and data source

We conducted a secondary analysis of cross-sectional data obtained from the most recent demographic and health surveys carried out from 2015 to 2022 in 44 low- and middle-income countries. The analysis included 25 countries from Africa, 15 from Asia, and 4 from other regions such as Latin America, Caribbean, and Europe.

### Study population and sample size

Initially, a total of 1,472,525 birth records (neonates) were identified in the 44 surveys appended for analysis, of which 991,581 had a missing observation on birth weight, 110,050 neonates were not weighed at birth, and 25,596 had unknown birth weight. After dropping records with missing observations and those with no birth weight data, a weighted sample of 343,898 birth records (unweighted sample size = 345,298) was included in the final analysis. ### Variables

#### Dependent variable

In this study, the dependent variable was birth weight, which was generated from the birth weight data measured in grams”. Thus, birth weights of less than 2500 g, 2500–3999 g, and > 4000 g were classified as low birth weight, normal birth weight, and excessive birth weight (macrosomia), respectively. We used the two classifications (low birth weight and others) for multivariable mixed-effect logistic regression model to identify the correlates of low birth weight. And we used three classifications for descriptive statistics to show the proportion of each class of birth weight in each country and region.

#### Independent variables

Individual-level variables included mother’s age, marital status, education and, media exposure, wealth index, coverage by health insurance, sex of neonate, age at marriage, parity, birth order, preceding birth interval, number of antenatal care (ANC) visits, timing of ANC visits, use of iron folic acid supplements, and history of pregnancy termination. While, region, residence, and distance to health facility were considered as the community-level variables.

Media exposure was computed using three variables (frequency of watching television, listening to the radio, and reading newspapers) that have three response options (i.e. not at all, less than once a week, and at least once a week). Thus, women who reported watching television, listening to the radio, or reading the newspaper at least once a week were considered as having media exposure and otherwise labeled as not having exposure to mass media.

### Data management and statistical analysis

Data cleaning and analysis were conducted using Stata software version 17. Prior to analysis, the presence of the outcome variable (i.e. weight at birth) in the DHS dataset for each country was confirmed, and all study variables were assessed for missing data. Birth records with missing observation and unknown birth weight, and those not weighted at birth were dropped from the analysis. Finally, the datasets of 44 LMIC countries were appended and weighted to compensate for the non-representativeness of the sample and obtain reliable estimates and standard errors.

To account for the hierarchical nature of DHS design, a multilevel logistic regression analysis was applied to determine the effects of independent variables on low birth weight. Initially, bivariable multilevel logistic regression analysis was done and variables with a p-value of less than 0.25 in this analysis were selected for the multivariable regression model.

### Fixed-effect multilevel analysis

Four hierarchical models were independently fitted to select the model that best fits the data. To test the random variability in the intercept, an empty model i.e. a model without an independent variable was fitted. In the second and third models, the effect of individual and community level variables on low birth weight was respectively assessed, while the combined effect of both community and individual level variables on the outcome variable was simultaneously assessed in the fourth model.

_Model I (empty model)_: in this model, the likelihood of low birth weight is only a function of the clusters in which the neonates reside, which is indicated by a random intercept at the cluster level:

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}\;(\mathrm{pi})=\log\;\mathrm{odds}=\left[\frac{\mathrm{pi}}{1\;-\;\mathrm{pi}}\right]\;=\;\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = log odds = \left[\frac{pi}{1 - pi}\right] = M + E_{A}
$$

Where M = overall mean prevalence of low birth weight expressed on the logistic scale. EA = cluster level residuals normally distributed on the logistic scale with a mean of 0 and a variance of VA. VA = the cluster residual variance represents the variability around the overall prevalence (M) on the logistic scale.

_Model II (a model with individual-level variables)_: this model measured the probability of low birth weight as a function of the cluster in which the neonates live and maternal and child characteristics (e.g. sex of child, maternal age, maternal education…etc.).

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}(\mathrm{pi})\;=\;\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_1\mathrm{sex}\;\mathrm{of}\;{\mathrm{child}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_2\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{age}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_3\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{education}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;\mathrm\beta4\dots\;.\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = M + \beta_{1} sex of child_{i} + \beta_{2} maternal age_{i} + \beta_{3} maternal education_{i} + \beta 4 \hdots . + E_{A}
$$

Where β is the regression coefficient of each individual-level variable included in this model.

_Model III (model with community-level variables)_: this model assessed the probability of low birth weight as a function of cluster and community-level variables (e.g. Region, residence, and distance to health facility).

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}(\mathrm{pi})=\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_1{\mathrm{region}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_2{\mathrm{residence}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_3{\mathrm{distance}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = M + \beta_{1} region_{i} + \beta_{2} residence_{i} + \beta_{3} distance_{i} + E_{A}
$$

Where β is the regression coefficient of each community-level variable included in this model.

_Model IV (model with both individual and community-level variables)_: in this model, the combined effect of both individual and community-level variables on the occurrence of low birth weight was simultaneously assessed.

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{Logit}(\mathrm{pi})\;=\;\mathrm M\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_1\mathrm{sex}\;\mathrm{of}\;{\mathrm{child}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_2\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{age}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_3\mathrm{maternal}\;{\mathrm{education}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;\mathrm\beta4\dots\;.{\mathrm\beta}_5{\mathrm{region}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_6{\mathrm{residence}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm\beta}_7{\mathrm{distance}}_{\mathrm i}\;+\;{\mathrm E}_{\mathrm A}$\end{document}

$$
Logit \left(\right. pi \left.\right) = M + \beta_{1} sex of child_{i} + \beta_{2} maternal age_{i} + \beta_{3} maternal education_{i} + \beta 4 \hdots . \beta_{5} region_{i} + \beta_{6} residence_{i} + \beta_{7} distance_{i} + E_{A}
$$

After fitting these models, models were compared based on log-likelihood (LL) and deviance (i.e. −2*LL) values to select the one that best fits the data. For instance, model IV has the lowest deviance and highest LL values and is hence considered as the best-fitted model for the final analysis. A generalized variance inflation factor [GVIF = VIF[1/(2*df)] was used to determine the presence of collinearity between explanatory variables and this value was less than five for all variables included in the final model, suggesting the non-existence of multi-collinearity. Finally, in the multivariable analysis, a _p_-value less than 0.05 and an adjusted odds ratio with the corresponding 95% confidence interval were used to identify determinants of low birth weight.

### Random-effect analysis (measures of variance)

Random variability in the level of low birth weight across clusters was estimated by intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC), proportion change in variance (PCV), and median odds ratio (MOR). In this analysis, ICC indicates the total variance in the proportion of low birth weight attributed to cluster differences. ICC was estimated by:

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{ICC}\;=\;\frac{{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}}{{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}\;+\;{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm i}}$\end{document}

$$
ICC = \frac{V_{a}}{V_{a} + V_{i}}
$$

Where, V a = cluster level variance and Vi = individual level variance.

PCV (attributable percentage variability in the multilevel model) measured the differences in the prevalence of low birth weight attributed to community or individual-level characteristics.

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{PCV}=\frac{\left[{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}\;-\;{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm b}\right]}{{\mathrm V}_{\mathrm a}}$\end{document}

$$
PCV = \frac{\left[V_{a}, ,-, ,V_{b}\right]}{V_{a}}
$$

Where V a = the variance of the empty model and V b = the variance of other models.

Heterogeneity in the risk of low birth weight among neonates in different clusters was assessed by MOR. It was measured as the median value of the odds of the outcome variable (i.e. low birth weight) between neonates living in the area at the highest risk of low birth weight compared to those in the clusters at the lowest risk of the event. MOR was computed using the following formula:

\documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \usepackage{upgreek} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document}$\mathrm{MOR}\;=\;\exp\;\left\{\sqrt{2\mathrm\tau}_0^2\mathrm\Phi\left(0.75\right)\right\}$\end{document}

$$
MOR = exp \left{\sqrt{2 \tau}_{0}^{2},\Phi,\left(0.75\right)\right}
$$

Where, Φ is the cumulative distribution function of a standard normal distribution, and Φ*(0.75) ~ 0.6745.

Data were obtained from a demographic and health survey, and permission to access it was granted through an online request process available at [http://www.dhsprogram.com](http://www.dhsprogram.com/). The accessed data were solely utilized for this registered study and can be publicly accessed from the program’s official database.

### Maternal obstetric and reproductive characteristics

Approximately one-third (33.3%) of births were to mothers who were married before the age of 18 and 7,137 (2.1%) births were reported as non-alive. More than half (56.4%) of births took place to multiparous mothers, 54,548 (15.9) were to mothers who had a history of pregnancy loss, and 92,665 (39.6%) were to mothers with shorter preceding birth intervals. ### Pooled and regional estimates of low birth weight in LMICs

Our analysis revealed that the overall prevalence of low birth weight births in low- and middle-income countries was estimated to be 13.7% [95% CI: 13.5%—13.8%], with significant variations across countries and regions. This finding indicates that, during the period from 2015 to 2022, there were a total of 46,988 low birth weight births recorded across 44 LMICs. The countries with the highest prevalence were Mauritania (25.0%), Pakistan (22.8%), India (17.7%), Haiti (17.1%), and Jordan (16.6%), while the lowest prevalence was observed in Sierra Leone (4.8%), Albania (4.9%), Armenia (5.7%), and Cambodia (6.1%). Regionally, Asia had the highest proportion of low birth weight births at 16%, followed by Latin America, the Caribbean, and Europe at 11.5%, and Africa at 9.5% (Fig.2).Fig. 2Regional and sub-regional estimates of low birth weight across 44 LMICs, 2015–2022

### Trend in low and excessive birth weight across 44 LMICs from 2015 to 2022

To examine the trend in the level of abnormal birth weight across 44 LMICs since 2015, countries were grouped based on the year of the survey. In this regard, from the surveys included in the analysis, six were conducted in 2015, eight in 2016, five in 2017, twelve in 2018/19, three in 2020, five in 2021, and six in 2022. Figure3 illustrates that the prevalence of low, excessive, and overall abnormal birth weight declined from 11.4% to 9.5%, 6.9% to 3.9%, and 18.3% to 13.5%, respectively over eight eight-year periods. However, the observed change did not follow consistent patterns, indicated by an increase in macrosomia by more than two-fold between 2021 and 2022 and an increase in the levels of both low and abnormal birth weight between 2020 and 2021 (Fig.3).Fig. 3Trend in low birth weight, macrosomia, and abnormal birth weight across 44 LMICs from 2015 to 2022

### Trend in low and excessive birth weight in 25 SSA countries from 2015 to 2022

Figure4 illustrates changes in birth weight across survey years in 25 African countries included in the analysis. For instance, both low and excessive birth weight declined from 10.2% to 8.5% and 8.3% to 5.2% over the survey periods respectively, however, the observed change was minimal for low birth weight compared to macrosomia. The result indicates that the most significant drop in low birth weight occurred between 2021 and 2022, while the largest decline of 50% in excessive birth weight was observed between 2016 and 2017 (Fig.4).Fig. 4Trend in low birth weight, macrosomia, and abnormal birth weight across 25 SSA countries from 2015 to 2022

### Trend in low and excessive birth weight in 15 Asian countries from 2015 to 2022

Variations in low and excessive birth weight in 15 Asian countries over different survey years are presented in Fig.5 below. The result revealed that consistent with changes observed in the African region, the trend in both abnormal birth weight indices has followed up-and-down patterns, with low birth weight decreasing from 15.8% to 10.9%, and excessive birth weight declining from 10.6% to 2.35%. Additionally, the results also underscore a consistent rise in the proportion of low birth weight births over three survey periods spanning from 2017 to 2021 (Fig.5).Fig. 5Trend in low birth weight, macrosomia, and abnormal birth weight across 15 Asian countries from 2015 to 2022

### Low and excessive birth weight across maternal characteristics

Figure6 shows the distribution of both low and excessive birth weight across maternal education and household wealth index. The analysis indicated a decrease in the proportion of low birth weight births as maternal age increases, dropping from 15.7% among younger women to 11.8% among those older than 34 years. On the contrary, the prevalence of excessive birth weight has increased as maternal age advances. Additionally, our findings highlighted a decline in low birth weight and a slight increase in macrosomic births with an improved household wealth index (Fig.6).Fig. 6Distribution of low and excessive birth weight across maternal age (**a**) and household wealth (**b**) in LMICs, 2015–2022

The result in Fig.7 shows a rise in the proportion of neonates with low birth weight as parity increases, with rates at 15.5% for first-time mothers compared to 11.8% for grand-multiparous women. Conversely, there was an uptick trend in the occurrences of macrosomic and overall abnormal birth weight births as parity progressed, with rates of 8.3% and 20.1% among grand-multiparous women, respectively. Additionally, our results indicate a decrease in both low and excessive birth weight births and their combinations as the frequency of antenatal visits increases (Fig.7).Fig. 7Distribution of low and excessive birth weight across maternal parity (**a**) and number of ANC visits (**b**) in LMICs, 2015–2022

Additionally, the measure of association (MOR) of 2.44 in the empty model suggested heterogeneity in the proportion of low birth weight births across clusters. ### Determinants of low birth weight in LMICs (Fixed-effect analysis)

After adjusting for the potential covariates, the result of a multilevel mixed-effect regression analysis showed a significant correlation between maternal characteristics and low birth weight. For instance, being not covered by health insurance [AOR (95% CI): 1.12 [1.06–1.18]], poor household wealth [AOR (95% CI): 1.15 [1.09–1.22]], younger maternal age [AOR (95% CI): 1.11 [1.02–1.21]], and facing challenges in accessing health facility [AOR (95% CI): 1.15 [1.11–1.19] were positively linked to low birth weight. Likewise, neonates born to mothers with no formal education [AOR (95% CI): 1.47 [1.33–1.63]], primary education [AOR (95% CI): 1.31 [1.19–1.44]], and secondary education [AOR (95% CI): 1.22 [1.12–1.33]] were at an increased risk of having low birth weight compared to those born to mothers with higher educational attainment. Furthermore, the analysis revealed that compared to their counter groups, neonates of mothers who did not receive prenatal care [AOR (95% CI): 1.35 [1.20–1.53]] or did not take antenatal iron supplementation [AOR (95% CI): 1.26 [1.10–1.45]] were about 35% and 26% more likely to have birth weight below the normal range, respectively (Table4).

## Discussion

The result showed that the pooled estimate of low birth weight in LMICs was 13.7% [95% CI: 13.5%—13.8%], with the highest prevalence in Mauritania (25.0%) and lowest in Sierra Leone (4.8%). This finding is consistent with the result of a study in six LMICs (13.6%) [14]. However, our finding is higher than the result of a study in 35 SSA countries (9.8%) [5], but slightly lower than the 2015 global estimate of 14.6% [4, 17]. The discrepancy between the results could be due to differences in data collection methods, sample sizes, or population demographics. Additionally, the slight variation from the global estimate could be due to regional differences in healthcare systems and socio-economic factors impacting maternal and child health outcomes.

The results of this study also show that beyond the individual characteristics of the participants, low birth weight is explained by contextual factors. For instance, the analysis revealed that newborns from households without health insurance had a 12% higher likelihood of being born with low birth weight compared to those born in households with health insurance coverage. This finding is supported by the previous studies that reported a significant link between health insurance coverage and reduced risk of low birth weight [18–20]. The most possible justification for this association is that women not enrolled in health insurance programs may not receive adequate prenatal care due to their lower socioeconomic status, which can directly affect pregnancy outcomes.

The sex of the neonates was also identified as one of the significant variables predicting low birth weight. For instance, compared to males, female neonates had a 30% higher likelihood of having low birth weight. Consistent with this finding, studies in SSA [5, 15] and a systematic review in Ethiopia [21] reported a higher risk of low birth weight among female neonates. This could be explained by the biological differences in fetal growth and development between genders. Studies have shown that female fetuses tend to have slower growth rates than males, which may increase their exposure to LBW [22].

Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the likelihood of low birth weight was 15% higher for newborns in poor households compared to those in rich households. Consistent with this, previous studies in different settings indicated a higher risk of low birth weight among neonates belonging to families of lower socioeconomic status [7, 15, 23, 24]. Socioeconomic disparities that can impact access to quality healthcare, nutrition, and overall living conditions can explain this finding. For instance, women in poor households may have limited access to prenatal care, inadequate nutrition, and higher levels of stress, which may result in poor pregnancy outcomes. Moreover, women from lower-income households are more likely to experience food insecurity and have limited access to essential nutrients during pregnancy, which can affect fetal growth and development.

Similar to the results of the studies conducted in SSA [15] and Kenya [25], this study found that infants of mothers who had difficulty accessing the nearest health facility were more likely to have babies with low birth weight when compared to their counterparts. This might be because women who face challenges in accessing healthcare facilities may experience delays in receiving essential prenatal care, screenings, and interventions, which can contribute to adverse birth outcomes such as LBW [26].

Lower maternal education was linked with an increased risk of low birth weight. The result showed that the risk of low birth weight was increased by 47%, 31%, and 22% for neonates born to mothers with no education, primary education, and secondary education, respectively. This finding is consistent with the previous studies in which maternal literacy was reported as a protective factor for low birth weight [5, 15, 27, 28]. This association could be because mothers with higher education may have better access to healthcare services and information that can promote healthier pregnancies and better birth outcomes. Additionally, higher education may be associated with greater knowledge about nutrition, prenatal care, and overall health practices that can positively impact fetal growth and development [29].

In addition, our analysis revealed that compared to their reference groups, neonates of mothers who did not have prenatal care were 1.35 times more likely to be born with low birth weight. Similarly, a study conducted in Ethiopia demonstrated that non-attendance of ANC was associated with an increased risk of LBW [21]. Likewise, other previous studies in African settings [5, 14, 15] found the attendance of antenatal care as a protective factor against LBW. This can be explained by the fact that the absence of prenatal care can lead to missed opportunities for interventions and support that are essential for promoting healthy pregnancies and reducing the risk of adverse outcomes such as LBW.

Prenatal nutritional supplementation was also identified as another important factor linked with low birth weight. The study showed that babies born to mothers who did not receive iron supplementation during pregnancy had a higher risk of low birth weight compared to those whose mothers took the supplement. This finding is consistent with studies conducted in Ethiopia, which indicated a lower chance of low birth weight among infants born to mothers who received this nutritional supplementation during pregnancy [11, 30]. This might be because maternal iron deficiency during pregnancy can lead to inadequate oxygen supply to the fetus, which may result in restricted growth [31].

### Strength and limitations

This study has several notable strengths, such as the utilization of a larger sample size, nationally representative multi-country data from 44 countries, and application of advanced statistical methods i.e. multilevel modeling to account for the nested structure of the DHS data. However, it is important to consider certain limitations when interpreting the findings. These include potential over or underestimation of estimates due to a large number of missing birth weight data in the original dataset, and differences in the number of countries and sample sizes in the regions included in the analysis might affect the regional estimates. Additionally, the study did not assess the influence of preconception and antenatal maternal nutritional status on the outcome variable due to a lack of available data in the DHS.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, the overall prevalence of LBW in LMICs was 13.7%, with notable variations in rates among countries and regions and a slight decline over time. The findings also showed that lack of health insurance, poor household wealth, younger maternal age, limited access to healthcare facilities, lower educational attainment, and inadequate prenatal care and iron supplementation were associated with an increased risk of LBW.

The reduction in LBW rates over eight years signifies some positive change, but the inconsistent patterns along with pre-existing socioeconomic and healthcare accessibility challenges highlight the need for context-specific actions. Important modifiable factors such as maternal education, prenatal care, antenatal iron supplements, and household wealth point toward the necessity of lowering structural imbalance and better maternal health services. Additionally, our finding suggests the need to focus on high-burden areas to lower LBW and the associated future health impacts.
